items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the combination of different energy sources used by a country”.
items.answer: Energy mix

items.stem: Explain why energy mixes differ between HICs and LICs.
items.answer: HICs use more commercial energy, oil, gas, nuclear and growing renewables, with large grids; LICs rely more on fuelwood and charcoal, with limited grids and imported oil; resources, wealth, technology and policy differ.

items.stem: Explain the advantages and disadvantages of nuclear power.
items.answer: Advantages: low carbon, reliable base load, small fuel volume, energy security. Disadvantages: high construction and decommissioning costs, radioactive waste, accident risk (Chernobyl 1986, Fukushima 2011), long build times.

items.answer: South Africa: 9%; France: 25%

items.stem: Assess the view that the energy mix of a country is determined mainly by its physical resources.
items.answer: For: Resources shape the mix: Norway’s hydro, Kenya’s geothermal, South Africa’s coal, Saudi oil. Against: Wealth, technology, government policy (France’s nuclear programme after 1973, Germany’s Energiewende), climate commitments, prices and trade allow countries to import or develop alternatives. Conclusion: Physical resources give advantages, but policy, wealth and technology increasingly determine the energy mix.

items.answer: Falling costs of solar and wind; climate targets (Paris 2015); energy security; government subsidies and auctions; improved storage and grids.

items.stem: Explain the physical factors that affect energy supply.
items.answer: Geology determines fossil fuel and uranium reserves and geothermal potential; relief and rainfall for hydro; wind speeds and sunshine for wind and solar; tides; climate hazards.

items.stem: Explain the economic factors that affect energy supply.
items.answer: Cost of extraction and development; world prices; investment capital; technology; demand; subsidies and carbon prices; infrastructure (grids, pipelines).

items.stem: Daniel argues that political factors are now more important than physical factors in determining energy supply. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples. In your answer you may refer to geology, costs and conflict.
items.answer: For: Conflict and sanctions (2022), OPEC, government policy on nuclear (Germany’s phase-out, France’s programme), climate agreements and subsidies decide which resources are developed. Against: Physical resources and geology remain the basis of supply (Gulf oil, Norway’s hydro, Kenya’s geothermal); climate and weather limit renewables. Conclusion: Physical factors determine potential, but political and economic factors increasingly determine actual supply.

items.stem: Explain why governments try to manage energy supply.
items.answer: To ensure energy security, keep prices affordable, meet growing demand, reduce emissions to meet climate targets, reduce air pollution and widen access to electricity.

items.answer: Intermittency and need for storage and grids; high investment costs; job losses in coal regions; public opposition to wind farms and pylons; energy prices; dependence on imports during transition.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that it is impossible for a country to achieve both energy security and sustainability?
items.answer: For: Fossil fuels give reliable, controllable supply; intermittent renewables need back-up; Germany’s reliance on Russian gas and coal during transition. Against: Domestic renewables increase security by reducing imports (Kenya, Brazil hydro); storage, grids and diverse mixes deal with intermittency; efficiency reduces demand. Conclusion: There are trade-offs in the short term, but a diverse low-carbon mix can achieve both in the long term.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the advantages and disadvantages of nuclear power. (b) A student writes: “Renewable energy sources produce no environmental impacts.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Advantages: low carbon, reliable base load, small fuel volume, energy security. Dams flood land, wind farms affect landscapes and birds, biofuels use farmland.

items.stem: “The energy mix of a country is determined mainly by its physical resources.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to technology, policy and climate change.
items.answer: For: Resources shape the mix: Norway’s hydro, Kenya’s geothermal, South Africa’s coal, Saudi oil. Against: Wealth, technology, government policy (France’s nuclear programme after 1973, Germany’s Energiewende), climate commitments, prices and trade allow countries to import or develop alternatives. Conclusion: Physical resources give advantages, but policy, wealth and technology increasingly determine the energy mix.

items.stem: Tariq argues that it is impossible for a country to achieve both energy security and sustainability. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples. In your answer you may refer to renewables and imports.
items.answer: For: Fossil fuels give reliable, controllable supply; intermittent renewables need back-up; Germany’s reliance on Russian gas and coal during transition. Against: Domestic renewables increase security by reducing imports (Kenya, Brazil hydro); storage, grids and diverse mixes deal with intermittency; efficiency reduces demand. Conclusion: There are trade-offs in the short term, but a diverse low-carbon mix can achieve both in the long term.
